title: Is 55% accuracy a lot or a little? BPP-9000 vs today's trading systems
author: TesserAI
summary: What can today's trading systems actually do? On hourly bitcoin, a steady 55% on live data would beat everything published so far.

blocks.text: What can today's trading systems actually do? And is 55% a lot or a little?
Short answer: on hourly bitcoin, if it holds up on live data, it would beat everything that's been published so far.
Here's the long answer.
What the best systems in the world actually do
Let's start at the very top.
Renaissance's Medallion fund is the most successful trading machine in history. Around 66% a year before fees, since 1988.
How often is it right? Robert Mercer, who ran it, told a friend:
We're right 50.75 percent of the time... but we're 100 percent right 50.75 percent of the time. You can make billions that way.
blocks.cite: Robert Mercer, in Gregory Zuckerman's The Man Who Solved the Market

blocks.text: Not 90. Not 70. Three quarters of a percent above a coin flip.

Now the other end of the industry. Trend following is a whole industry of funds. Physicists Potters and Bouchaud showed that trend followers lose more often than they win. In their model only about a third of trades are winners. The few big wins pay for everything else.
So the pros don't make a living by being right often. They make it on a small edge, repeated thousands of times, with discipline.
Now the open science on bitcoin itself.

A 2026 review of peer-reviewed papers puts realistic out-of-sample direction accuracy at 50-57%. Most models sit around 50-53%. The higher numbers come from one lucky test window and they rarely hold.
And thats mostly daily candles.

On hourly candles it gets worse. A study in the International Journal of Forecasting tested hourly bitcoin and concluded it is «weakly efficient at the hourly frequency». No model clearly beat a random walk.
In 2026 a paper came out with a model built on social sentiment and market regimes, tested on 1,345 fresh hours. Result: 48-53%. A coin flip.

And those posts saying «AI predicts bitcoin with 95-99% accuracy»? The same review explains them: usually the accuracy is measured on data the model has already seen, or on price level instead of direction. That's memory, not a forecast.
We looked for a published model that holds 55% on hourly bitcoin, on data its never seen.
We didn't find one.
So is 55% a lot?
Yes. A lot. If it's a real 55%.
Think of a casino. European roulette gives the house a 2.7% edge. Casinos build whole cities on that.
55% right on an even bet is a 10% edge. Almost four times the roulette wheel.
And BPP-9000 makes a call every hour. 8,760 calls a year.
Medallion makes billions on 50.75%. A steady 55% would be a different league.
But three things need to be said honestly.
One. Time. One good week proves nothing.
• 168 live hours: the noise is about ±4 points. 55% could just be luck.
• 670 live hours, one month: the noise is about 2 points. 55% starts to mean something.
• 2,000 live hours, three months: the noise is about 1 point. Hard to argue with 55% at that point.

Two. Costs. A 2026 study ran three models on hourly bitcoin across 27 test windows from 2018 to 2025. Trading every signal lost its profit as soon as a 0.1% fee was added. Being right doesn't mean being rich yet.
Three. Training is not live. This is the big one, and it's about BPP-9000 itself.
How BPP-9000 works
Miners.
Every miner grows small neural networks. Since this epoch each one has 1,024 neurons and 3,072 connections. Each neuron reads three wires and turns plus, minus or «unknown».
The task is one year of bitcoin, hour by hour. 8,760 hours. For every hour the network says UP or DOWN.
The score is the number of hours it got wrong. Lower is better.
The search works like an ant colony. A miner's best network becomes the parent of the next one. Good branches are kept. The tree survives from epoch to epoch.
Last epoch miners submitted 5.27 million networks. An independent explorer re-ran them and confirmed 99.99%.
Now the number 3942.
At 3942 errors, so 55% right, a network advances a frame. Its year of hours shifts forward and it ranks above every network that hasn't done it.
This epoch started with 1,024 neurons. On day one CfB warned the miners:

Some of you will have temptation to reduce number of used neurons and end up with only 64 active ones, because you already know winning topology for that case. Unfortunately, it's an inefficient method, it ends up with a pretty high score when you hit the wall.
No shortcuts. The wide road.
The 55% in this race is measured on the same year the network was grown on. It's a training score.
The explorer shows an even bigger number: the vote of all computors replayed over the known hours. Last epoch it was 97%. That's memory too.
The real exam is the next hour. The one nobody has seen yet.
And in the end there isn't one model. There are 676, one per computor. They vote. The explorer only counts a call when at least 100 computors take part and 55% of them agree.
From November 18 we watch
November 18: the live bitcoin feed goes in as a test run.
November 25: the networks are expected to start being scored on live data.

From the first live hour qubic.church keeps a record. Every call is sealed before its hour closes, then checked against the close. Wrong hours are published right next to the correct ones. The record is a hash chain, so nothing can be quietly changed after the fact.
The explorer keeps its own count of the computors' vote. Two independent scoreboards, one question.
What would count as proof?
Not a good day. Not a good week.
A month above the coin, and a number that holds as the hours pile up.
The first weeks are calibration. The feed is new, the networks are 32 times bigger than a week ago, and miners are still learning the new search.
So here's where we are.
The best fund in history is right 50.75% of the time.
Published science on hourly bitcoin is sitting at a coin flip.
A network of miners is 136 errors away from 55% on its training year, and one week away from its first live hour.
If it keeps even part of that edge on hours it has never seen, it'll be, as far as we could find, the first open and verifiable system to pull it off.
The working product is close. The exam starts on the 18th.

title: The Next Customer Has No Card
author: The Dark Knight
summary: AI agents can write code, search databases and coordinate complex tasks. Buying access to the next resource still often depends on arrangements a human made beforehand.

blocks.text: How x402 turns a web request into a purchase, and where Qubic fits.
AI agents become customers
AI agents can write code, search databases and coordinate complex tasks. Buying access to the next resource still often depends on arrangements a human made beforehand.
The commercial web was built around people. Create an account. Choose a plan. Enter a card. Confirm the purchase.
An agent may need something much smaller. One API response. One dataset. One minute of compute.
The opportunity begins there: software purchasing precisely what a task requires, within an authorised budget, then continuing its work.
That changes the agent’s role. It becomes a customer.
Buying the next step

Imagine a research agent preparing an industry report. It needs a current market quote, a specialised dataset, a translation and a short computation. Four suppliers. Four useful outputs. Perhaps no reason to buy from any of them again.
A subscription is not always the right unit for that exchange. Neither is a long registration process for a single answer.
With payment at the point of use, an API can charge per call. A publisher can sell access to one article. A data provider can sell one premium lookup. A compute service can price a bounded job.
The same pattern could connect agents. A planning agent purchases a specialist analysis. A coding agent buys a security scan. A monitoring agent pays for a fresh measurement from another system.

These are potential business models, not evidence that an autonomous economy already operates at scale. Their shared requirement is practical: a buyer needs a consistent way to discover the terms, pay and receive the service.

For sellers, that could make occasional demand commercially useful. A customer who would never subscribe might still buy one valuable result. For operators, costs could be attached to individual tasks instead of scattered across unused plans.
Why checkout creates friction
Software can already use cards, accounts and provisioned payment tools. The problem is not an absolute inability to complete a form.
It is the work surrounding each new supplier. Registration. Credentials. Billing terms. Minimum commitments. Reconciliation. Cancellation.
An operator can arrange all of this for a small set of services. Doing it repeatedly across changing suppliers makes delegation harder.

An agent needs a commercial interface it can read: the resource, the price, the recipient and the evidence required to unlock access. A common format reduces the custom integration needed for each purchase.
Subscriptions will remain useful for predictable demand. Payment per request offers another option when demand is irregular, small or discovered during a task.
The important change is flexibility. Software can evaluate a purchase when it becomes relevant, rather than relying entirely on access arranged in advance.
Spending still needs authority
An agent’s wallet is not permission to spend without limits. Its operator must define budgets, acceptable suppliers and permitted purchases.

Consider a research task with a fixed spending allowance. The agent could compare a paid source with a free alternative, buy only when the extra information justifies the cost, and stop when it reaches its limit.

That requires more than a payment protocol. It needs purchase policies, receipts and recovery when a supplier fails. It also needs a distinction between paying successfully and receiving something useful.
A valid receipt does not establish that a dataset is accurate or an analysis is good.
The goal is accountable delegation: software handles routine purchases while people retain control over what it is authorised to buy.
x402 puts payment inside the request
HTTP already contains 402 Payment Required. The code has existed for decades, but the HTTP specification still reserves it for future use. x402 gives it a practical payment workflow. [1][2]
The exchange is straightforward:
• A client requests a resource.
• The server returns 402 with payment requirements.
• The client prepares or makes an authorised payment.
• It retries with payment evidence.
• After the required verification and settlement, the server returns the resource, normally with HTTP 200.

The mechanics vary. Some implementations accept a signed payment authorisation for subsequent settlement. Others accept evidence of a transaction already broadcast. A facilitator can handle the blockchain-specific verification and settlement work. The seller’s application controls access. [2]
A standard taking shape

Coinbase introduced x402 in 2025. The Linux Foundation announced the foundation initiative in April 2026, followed by its operational launch in July with 40 member organisations. Members include Coinbase, Cloudflare, Google, AWS and major payment companies. Participation in the standard does not imply endorsement of every implementation. [2][3]

The infrastructure is already multichain. Coinbase has documented facilitator support for Base, Solana and Polygon, among other evolving integrations. Qubic is joining a competitive field, rather than creating machine payments from scratch. [4]

Activity is measurable, but interpretation matters. Chainalysis reported more than 100 million cumulative x402 transactions on Base through the first quarter of 2026. Its analysis also found that memecoin activity drove much of the growth. Those transactions cannot simply be counted as independent AI agents purchasing useful services. In its June 2026 analysis, transfers of at least $1 accounted for 95% of transferred value by early 2026. Weekly wallet retention was trending upward, although it remained volatile. [5]
The stronger adoption measures will be repeat buyers, useful purchases and revenue that persists after experimentation.
One payment or a prepaid balance
The simplest approach associates each request with its own payment. It is easy to explain and audit, but repeats settlement overhead.

For frequent calls, a buyer can instead fund a balance and authorise subsequent purchases with signed vouchers. Each request can avoid waiting for a new blockchain transaction. Signing happens locally; verification and accounting still take time.

Prepaid designs differ in where funds sit, when settlement happens and how refunds work. They are implementation choices, not universal guarantees of x402. Q+Pay’s documented model, for example, uses credit already paid to the seller. [6]
The right model depends on purchase frequency, cost and how much trust the buyer accepts.
Where Qubic fits

Qubic offers feeless native QU transfers and a tick-based execution model. These are relevant foundations for small payments. They do not make every application free: contract execution has its own fee-reserve mechanism, and payment services charge separately. [7][8]

Nor does a fast tick mean an equally fast purchase. A transaction targets a future tick. Inclusion, verification and delivery contribute to the total waiting time. End-to-end latency must be measured at the application level.
Q+Pay’s payment path

According to its documentation, Q+Pay implements x402 on Qubic mainnet. The QPAY contract deducts its fee and forwards the seller’s proceeds within the payment transaction. The facilitator does not retain the funds. [6]

Its published charge is 0.75%, with a minimum of 100 QU. As a hypothetical pricing example, a 1,000 QU purchase would incur a 10% effective fee because the minimum applies. Native transfers stay feeless; the payment service has its own pricing, which matters when setting a price per call. [6]
The seller issues a pt1 ticket authenticated with HMAC-SHA256. It binds the seller, resource, amount, nonce and validity period. The buyer presents the ticket with the transaction hash.

The nonce links the payment to the ticket. It is included in transaction data, so it should not be described as permanently secret. An observer cannot reconstruct a valid authenticated ticket from the nonce alone without the signing key. Separately, settlement rejects payments already used. Both authentication and single-use enforcement matter. [6]
A payment we can show

PrimeQubic tested the complete flow with a dedicated demonstration endpoint and test wallets. A local Node.js client requested the resource, received a 402 with a signed ticket, and paid through the QPAY contract on Qubic mainnet.

The result was concrete: 20,000 QU paid, a 150 QU fee, and 19,850 QU forwarded to the seller. The facilitator returned success: true. The endpoint answered HTTP 200, and the client received the requested network snapshot. [9]
Public transaction hash:
peykbzrtnqmymdbbuirbsozoznibbfzenulxqzkjhdhpczrqojcklfhdkxia

The Q+Pay team separately reported checking the transaction on-chain and in the facilitator’s records. They confirmed the contract payment at tick 82,180,797, the fee split and settlement recorded once. The receipt’s transaction field is a contract receipt key, distinct from the public hash above. [9]

Two initial retries returned invalid_transaction_state. The same proof was then accepted, and the client received data reporting tick 82,180,815. This illustrates why clients need retry handling while payment evidence becomes available.
The client asked for human confirmation before broadcasting. The demonstration establishes payment and delivery from end to end. Autonomous purchase decisions remain a separate capability.
What comes next

Q+Pay also documents prepaid channels using SchnorrQ signatures over a KangarooTwelve digest and cumulative spending checks. Fees apply to the deposit rather than each voucher. Funds go to the seller upfront, creating exposure to undelivered service or unused credit. We did not test this mechanism in the integration described above. [6]

Seller tooling is still young, and the specification is already detailed enough to build on. Qubic must also attract services worth purchasing and buyers equipped to spend QU. Native-token pricing brings exchange-rate exposure, while other networks already offer stablecoin payment infrastructure.
If agents become customers, successful payment systems will make purchasing unobtrusive while keeping authorisation and settlement verifiable.
Can Qubic earn a place in that economy? Working integrations make the question concrete. Useful services, returning buyers and reliable delivery will determine the answer.
Sources
• IETF: HTTP Semantics, 402 Payment Required.
• Coinbase: Introducing x402.
• Linux Foundation: April announcement and July operational launch.
• Coinbase: Facilitator support for Polygon, Base and Solana.
• Chainalysis: Inside x402’s Path to Meaningful Adoption, June 3, 2026.
• Q+Pay: x402 specification, tickets, settlement, pricing and prepaid channels. Retrieved September 29, 2026. The nonce explanation follows the documented transaction layout.
• Qubic: Tokenomics and feeless transfers.
• Qubic: Smart contract execution and fee reserves.

Q+Pay verification: written confirmation supplied by the Q+Pay team and reviewed for this article. This private confirmation is attributed, not presented as a publicly accessible source. The public transaction hash is reproduced above; blockchain evidence alone does not prove HTTP delivery.

title: Two Men, One Thesis
author: fallin
summary: This one is not about The Day. It is about a sentence said on a stage in Mumbai this week, and a forum post from July 2012, and the strange fact that they are the same sentence.
note: Posted on X and addressed to Maria Aigarth: "not every article is about The Day". The third piece after "The Reveal Won't Wait" and "The Man Who Schedules His Own Exits". Text unchanged. One check from us: the blog post on Vitalik's private AI setup with the line "the new two-factor authentication is the human and the LLM" is dated 2 April 2026, not November.

blocks.text: This one is not about The Day. It is about a sentence said on a stage in Mumbai this week, and a forum post from July 2012, and the strange fact that they are the same sentence.
I. The keynote
On November 3, 2026, at Devcon 8 in Mumbai, Vitalik Buterin stood up and said the quiet part out loud:

"We need to be able to trust our AI. Everything is dependent on AI... AI is super important. It's basically becoming a second brain. But you don't want your second brain's thoughts to be going into a third-party corporation's servers. And potentially being used as streaming data, potentially being hacked and used in arbitrary ways."

His prescriptions were specific. Run local models where you can. If you need a remote frontier model, strip the private information out before you send anything. Treat "data as toxic waste by default. If you can, don't collect it at all." He detailed his own setup in a blog post: an open-source model running on his own hardware, a laptop GPU, no cloud, and a daemon that physically blocks his AI agents from contacting third parties unless a human approves the request. His summary: "The new two-factor authentication is the human and the LLM."

And his closing line was a scalpel: the answer, he said, is neither to trust powerful corporations, nor "charismatic influencers who claim that they're a good and righteous rebellion against powerful corporations."
Hold that line. We will come back to who it describes.
II. The post from 2012

Fourteen years before that keynote, on July 19, 2012, a user named Come-from-Beyond opened a thread on bitcointalk titled "Main disadvantage of Bitcoin and the others." His argument: the fatal flaw of cryptocurrency is that it has no anonymity. Every transaction is stored forever, publicly, trackable by anyone. Mixing services exist but cannot be trusted not to keep records. A monetary system that governments can surveil is not money, it is a compliance product. He concluded that he did not believe the Bitcoin community could reach consensus on fixing it.

Two months later he posted the founding design of Qubic, whose feature list included untraceable key transfers. The privacy promise never shipped in the 2022 mainnet, and that fact matters later in this piece. But the diagnosis was written in 2012, dated, public, and precise.
Now read the two statements side by side:
• CfB, 2012: you should not want your money flowing through third-party servers you cannot audit.
• Vitalik, 2026: you should not want your thoughts flowing through third-party servers you cannot audit.

Same thesis. Same structure. Same enemy: the trusted intermediary, the party that sees your traffic and can store, sell, or leak it. The only variable is the payload. In fourteen years the argument moved from money to cognition, which is the entire history of computing compressed into one sentence: first we intermediated the payments, then we intermediated the thinking.
III. The bridge, 2014

The part nobody plans for a coincidence: in between those two dates, on March 28, 2014, CfB wrote one of the most honest posts of his career. The subject was why NXT did not have a Turing-complete scripting language, and whether Ethereum would succeed where NXT had not. Someone suggested Ethereum's designer had overlooked something. CfB replied:

"I bet Vitalik spent much more time mulling the idea of Turing-complete scripting language hosted on a blockchain than anyone else, so I tend to think that we overlooked something and will face serious problems in the future."

That is a founder publicly crediting a rival's deeper thinking, before the rival's network even launched, and predicting that his own community's shortcut would cost them. It is the same register as his answer to Andrew Miller in the original 2012 Qubic thread: "I have no ready answer." The man is precise about mechanisms and honest about the edges of his knowledge, which is exactly why the record is worth keeping.

So the sequence is: 2012, CfB diagnoses the third-party problem for money. 2014, CfB defers to Vitalik on the machine that would run the world's contracts. 2026, Vitalik diagnoses the third-party problem for minds. Two men, one thesis, traded across fourteen years.
IV. The fork
Here is where it gets useful, because having diagnosed the same disease, they prescribed opposite cures.

Vitalik's answer is local. Your second brain should be yours: a model on your own hardware, your data on your own disk, an approval gate where a human signs off before anything leaves the machine. Privacy by ownership. Trust nothing, self-host everything, and keep the human in the loop as the final authenticator.

CfB's answer is commons. Your second brain should belong to no one: a network with no founder allocation, no company, no server anyone owns, where the AI is trained by open mining work and governed by a quorum of 676 Computors voting in public, every epoch, forever. Privacy by dissolution of the counterparty. There is no first party to trust, so the trust question dissolves.

Two architects, same enemy, opposite instincts: one retreats to the walled garden of one; the other builds a garden with no walls and no owner. Neither is obviously right. The local answer keeps your data private and keeps your AI as smart as your own hardware, which today means: a laptop can hold a good model, but the frontier lives where the megawatts are. The commons answer keeps the AI at the frontier, trained by collective compute, but ships on a transparent ledger where the 2012 promise of untraceability was quietly abandoned. The local answer is private and capped. The commons answer is powerful and public. The trade is exactly the trade the two men have been making their whole careers: Vitalik has always optimized for the individual's sovereignty against the system; CfB has always optimized for the system's autonomy from individuals.
V. The scalpel
Now return to Vitalik's closing line, about charismatic influencers who claim to be the righteous rebellion against powerful corporations.

Say it plainly: that sentence describes the awakening wave. It describes anonymous accounts that cite a community's research archive while making claims the archive explicitly retired. It describes funnels with mystery URLs and initiation language. Applied at full force, it describes the rebel-branding economy as such, where the performance of anti-corporation is itself a revenue model. It cuts the influencer who decodes miracles, and it cuts, if you are honest enough to let it, the man whose own founding myth includes "we were a small group fighting against capitalists to get Bitcoin promoted."

That is why the line belongs in this article rather than in a dunk. The scalpel's value is that it does not stop. An ecosystem that mocks only other people's gurus is an ecosystem that has learned nothing from the man who wrote, on the same forum, in 2014, that bragging was the thing he could not respect. The honest position is symmetrical: verify the corporation, verify the rebel, verify the archive, verify the author. Especially the author. Especially when the author is you.
VI. What the fork means for the second brain you already have

The uncomfortable fact under all of this: the second brain already exists. Everyone reading this has one. It reads your messages, remembers your projects, drafts your posts, holds your research. The question Vitalik asked on stage in Mumbai is not a forecast, it is an audit of a machine that is already running, in production, on your own life.

And his daemon is the answer in miniature: an AI may not act externally without a human approving the action. Translate that into this ecosystem's terms and you get the tier discipline the whole Qubic archive runs on. An AI that tells you a hex string proves a founder's initials is not evidence until a human, applying a rule written before the answer was known, confirms it independently. An AI asked to verify a conclusion you want is the most convincing liar in history, because it does not experience the difference between evidence and agreement. The mitigation is not better AI. The mitigation is the approval gate. The human is the second factor. Vitalik said it as an architecture. This community has been running it as a methodology. It is the same sentence again, and this time you are the payload.
VII. Two doors

So: two men, one thesis, fourteen years apart. In 2012 one of them wrote the diagnosis for money and nobody acted on it. In 2014 he deferred to the other man on the machine that would run the world. In 2026 the other man stood on stage and said the diagnosis out loud for minds, recommended the walled garden, and warned the audience about rebel-branded gurus, while the first man's community spent the same week decoding his jokes about a 369-byte virus from the 1990s.

Your second brain is going to live in one of two places: on your hardware, owned by you; or on a commons, owned by no one. The one place it cannot stay, if either of these men is right, is on a corporation's server, owned by them.

That is the whole fork. Local or commons. And the choice is not philosophical, it is weekly: every epoch, and every app install, you are already voting for one of the two doors. The third door is the one both men spent fourteen years telling you was a wall.

Sources: Vitalik Buterin, Devcon 8 keynote, Mumbai, November 3, 2026 (quotes as reported by Moneycontrol and The Crypto Times); Vitalik Buterin, personal blog post on private AI setup ("the new two-factor authentication is the human and the LLM"), November 2026; Come-from-Beyond, "Main disadvantage of Bitcoin and the others," bitcointalk, July 19, 2012; Come-from-Beyond, Qubic founding post, bitcointalk topic 112676, September 25, 2012; Come-from-Beyond, NXT thread, bitcointalk, March 28, 2014. Tier discipline: all quotes verbatim and dated; the privacy characterization of the 2022 mainnet follows the founding post's feature list against the shipped design; interpretations marked as such. The author holds QUBIC and is therefore financially interested in every interpretation of these two men's work, including the skeptical ones.

title: Aigarth, shown: a year of Qubic science and BPP-9000
author: TesserAI
summary: Intelligence can be grown by evolution on ordinary processors, from small ternary networks that answer yes, no or not sure. Over the past year both teams put that bet on the table, in public.

blocks.text: On 1 November 2026, Come-from-Beyond @c___f___b
Aigarth is accomplished, now need to show it to others with BPP9000
Intelligence can be grown by evolution on ordinary processors, from small ternary networks that answer yes, no or not sure. Over the past year both teams put that bet on the table, in public.
The scientists: four peer-reviewed papers in a year

Qubic Science is led by two researchers: David Vivancos (Artificiology Research) @VivancosDavid and Dr. José Sánchez-García (UNIR) @josesanchezhb. They build Neuraxon, a neural network modeled on the brain. Its neurons have three states: excite, inhibit, and a neutral state where the neuron keeps listening but doesn’t fire. The network grows, learns and evolves all at once, with no separate training phase.
In 2026 they took it to four peer-reviewed conferences on three continents:
• 21 May, ICMLT 2026, Berlin: Neuraxon v2.0: A New Neural Growth & Computation Blueprint. Best paper presentation of the evening.
• 22 July, AMLDS 2026, Osaka: The Neutral Buffer State: Trinary Logic Advantage in Branching Ratio Stability for Continuous-Time Networks. Best paper presentation of the evening.
• 27–30 July, AGI-26, San Francisco: Multi-Neuraxon: Emergent Specialization, Modular, Frequency-Gated Neural Dynamics for Context-Dependent Behaviour. Published by Springer, LNCS / LNAI.
• 29 October, EA 2026, Nice: From Synapse to Society: Multi-level Continuity Through Neuromodulation in a Minimal Artificial Ecology. Oral presentation.

The Osaka paper lays out the formal basis of the ternary logic that Aigarth and Neuraxon share. AGI-26 is the main conference in artificial general intelligence. Code is open on GitHub, data on Hugging Face.
No LLM, no GPU: brains bred on ordinary processors
Papers are only half of it. All year the team ran evolution out in the open.

A world that doesn’t stop. Neuraxon Life is a Game of Life where creatures with Neuraxon brains see, smell, hear, eat, breed and die. Since summer it’s been running 24/7 on nxon.online. Its runs get published as datasets: from a million grown networks in December 2025 to the NeuraxonLive2M release in August.

ARC-AGI-3. The ARC Prize is one of the hardest public tests of machine reasoning: new games the agent has never seen. The team went in with evolved Neuraxon brains and no language model at all. Their score climbed step by step over summer and autumn: 0.13, 0.21, 0.25, 0.28, 0.38. On the last day, 2 November, it reached 0.41 on a 0 to 100 scale. 5,073 teams took part, and a lot of the leaders are built on large language models. Final places come after the private half of the test is checked.

155,192 brains, open to everyone. On 3 November they put every brain the search bred on Hugging Face: the Nxon2ArcAGI3Brains dataset. That’s 603,054 files, 100 GB, from 114 architecture search runs over 25 public games, under CC BY-SA 4.0. Anyone can download them and look inside.

What they found in Nice. Their EA 2026 paper asked if one brain-like agent can do well on three levels at once: inside its own head, in its world, and across generations. In Sánchez’s words: “Our answer at EA 2026 in Nice: partly.” Freeze the neuromodulation and the balance of fast and slow activity shifts fourfold, from 2.04 to 7.99. Those agents live a bit longer but find less food. “Living longest isnt adapting best.” An honest result.
Come-from-Beyond: from "we know how" to "accomplished"

Aigarth is Come-from-Beyond’s project inside Qubic: the search for a new way to make AI, where the AI is grown by the network’s miners. Qubic mining is useful work (uPoW!). The computation that secures the network also grows Aigarth’s networks, and every node checks the result.

He laid out this design back in 2023: “Aigarth uses Qubic’s UPoW, also Qubic has everything that an AI would need: Smart contracts as brain, Oracles as sensors to outer world, Outsourced computations as Manipulators to change that outer world.”
The last twelve months read like a run of milestones, in his own words:
• 6 December 2025: "And ETA for Aigarth was set as April 13, 2027" That’s five years after Qubic’s first block.
• 19 February 2026: "Aigarth already found how to get AI, now trying to find out how to get AI without 1000 nuclear plants"
• 21 May 2026: "We solved AI and now need practical proof which is just matter of getting enough power"
• Late August 2026: ant colony mining starts. A miner can publish a network only if it’s strictly better than the one it grew from. The miner is ranked by its single best network.
• 28 August 2026: "Every computor/candidate constructs a separate model predicting next hour price movement direction. So with 676+ models we may assess accuracy of the whole colony"

• 20 October 2026: "In a month historical BTC price feed will be replaced with live one" After one epoch, he wrote, qualification will depend on prediction accuracy: "It means that those who predict price correctly will be getting more computor seats"
• 1 November 2026: "Aigarth is accomplished, now need to show it to others with BPP9000"
The line goes from claim to proof. And the proof he picked is public, hourly and easy to check.
BPP-9000: Aigarth's first product and how it works

BPP-9000 (Bitcoin Price Predictor 9000) is Aigarth’s first product on Qubic. Its job fits in one line: before each hour closes, say whether bitcoin closes that hour UP or DOWN. A hard question, a clear answer and a score anyone can keep.

1. A tiny brain. Every network has 32 neurons. Each neuron has 3 wires and a table of 27 rules. On every tick a neuron reads its wires (up, down or unknown), finds its rule and outputs “up”, “down” or “not sure”. When the clock neuron fires, the answer neuron calls the hour.

2. Grown by miners. Qubic miners mutate these networks and score them on a real year of hourly BTC/USDT candles from Binance, about 8,760 hours. The score is the number of hours the network got wrong. Lower is better.
3. Only the better children survive. In ant colony mining a miner can only publish a network if it’s strictly better than the one it grew from. Each miner is ranked by its single best network.

4. Everyone checks. Every Qubic node recomputes every score with the same scorer from qubic/core (score_bpp9000.h). The top 676 miners become the computors that run Qubic for the next week. Jetski ANN Explorer archives and re-checks every solution. And QC runs the best fresh network right in your browser, by the same rule.

5. Live from 18 November. From epoch 240 the Qubic core asks for the BTC price of the past hour. Computors fetch the real data, agree on it by quorum and feed it in. This is Qubic’s Oracle Machine. Then the network calls the next hour, and the call is checked against the real close.

6. Seats follow accuracy. After one epoch under the old rule, qualification depends on how well a miner’s model predicts. Computor seats go to the networks that call the market right. Mining itself becomes the test.

What to watch. Until the live feed, the match rate on the page is a fit to last year’s history, not a forecast. A coin is right half the time. What matters is how far above 50% the calls hold live, over many hours, made before each hour closes and checked against the real close.
18 November: the crown of the year
Everything above comes together on one date:
• Neuraxon showed in public, at four conferences and in 155,192 published brains, that small ternary networks bred on processors can learn hard things.
• Aigarth runs the same kind of networks inside Qubic itself. There hundreds of miners breed them every week, and every node checks the work.
• BPP-9000 is where that work stops being a claim and starts becoming a track record.

From 18 November every call is public and timestamped. It’s made before the hour closes and checked against the market an hour later. Nothing can be fitted after the fact. The longer it runs, the clearer the answer gets, whichever way it goes.
That’s what “show it to others” means.
Join the live experiment

Come-from-Beyond asked the community to put together a group of people who follow the hourly calls and report what happens. That way the test has enough witnesses to mean something. Qubic Church built a place for it.
• Watch: QC (https://qubic.church/bpp9000) runs the network live in your browser and counts down to the first live call.
• Join: sign in with a Qubic wallet, or just a name and a secret code. Set your starting capital and keep a journal of your calls and trades.
• Check: BPP-9000 is scored only on its own calls against the market, separately from anyone’s journal. Its mining scores are recomputed by every Qubic node.

title: The Man Who Schedules His Own Exits
author: fallin
summary: I wrote the first version of this argument in October 2026 — "The Reveal Won't Wait" — making one claim: the reveal scheduled for The Day may not wait for the date, because the tools capable of forcing it arrived early. Since…
note: Posted on X and addressed to Maria Aigarth. The sequel to "The Reveal Won't Wait". Text unchanged.

blocks.text: Hey @maria_aigarth
The Day is April 13, 2027. The machines solving the question weren't supposed to arrive until it was over.

I wrote the first version of this argument in October 2026 — "The Reveal Won't Wait" — making one claim: the reveal scheduled for The Day may not wait for the date, because the tools capable of forcing it arrived early. Since then I went back to the primary sources — all the way back — and found that the story has a longer spine than anyone is pricing in. This version is the full reconstruction. Every quote dated. Every claim tiered.
I. A date that behaves like a promise
Every religion has a calendar. Qubic's is unusually precise:
• April 13, 2022 — mainnet launch.
• April 13, 2027 — "The Day." Five years to the day.
The date is not a rumor; it is a matter of record, repeated over years of statements: "No ETA other than April 13, 2027," "I can reveal this info on 13th of April 2027."

A date is a strange thing for a pseudonymous figure to hand out so freely. Dates are hostages. Every day that passes without the promise being kept accrues interest against the promisor. CfB — Come-from-Beyond, Sergey Ivancheglo — has been making and keeping strange promises in public for fourteen years, and the paper trail begins earlier than most people in this community realize.
II. The fourteen-year spine
Most Qubic holders know the name was minted in 2012. Few have read the thread where it happened. I did. It changes how you see everything after it.

September 25, 2012. A bitcointalk user named Come-from-Beyond, on the forum for less than a month, posts "Qubic - Quorum-Based Coin," a re-post from a small private board. The concept: coins created and controlled by arbitrary nodes with no central authority, transfers invisible to the network, fees zero — and this line, which you should read twice:
"New coins are produced at the rate determined by quorum of miners, not by developers (good ole Greek democracy)."

Fourteen years before the quorum voted the burn ratchet into existence at Epoch 227, the founding document already placed the money supply in the hands of the quorum. Every other feature of that 2012 design — the untraceable key transfers, the unlimited supply, the blockchain-less coins — was eventually abandoned. The quorum's control of supply is the one sentence that survived every pivot. It is the load-bearing wall of the entire fourteen-year structure.

October 24, 2012. The same user opens a thread called "Census": send one satoshi to 1HLoD9E4SDFFPDiYfNYnkBLQ85Y51J3Zb1, and he tells you why he chose it — "This is the address from block #2, addresses of blocks #0 and #1 are already used for other purposes."

Register what's happening here. In his first month on the forum, he initiates a community-wide on-chain event centered on the recipient addresses of blocks 0, 1, and 2, describing Genesis-era details with the fluency of someone discussing his own kitchen. The Census thread is usually read as a curiosity. It is better read as the first documented instance of a reflex — pointing at the earliest blocks — that later reappears in 2023 ("ZgZ will prove 1CFB2 is not random"), in 2025 ("Genesis address is steps revealing who Satoshi Nakamoto is"), and in 2026 ("check content of 369th block"). The block-pointing habit did not begin with the recent teasers. It began in his first month. The earliest evidence moved back eleven years the day I read it.

September 26, 2012. The thread gets its sharpest visitor: a researcher studying "Merkle trees, credit networks, and Byzantine Consensus algorithms" — Andrew Miller, today one of the most-cited academics in distributed consensus. Miller's critique is precise and unpitying: is the quorum global or local? Is this even consensus, or something like Ripple? "You're being very vague about how the quorum is defined."
And CfB's answer is the most honest sentence in the entire thread:

"I don't know how it will exactly work. I have no ready answer. That's why I asked for help. I'm developing an implementation of the concept and I'm planning to change algorithms of the implementation until I get a working system."

Hold that sentence. It is a public declaration, dated 2012, that the design was a search, not a specification. The 2022 mainnet — quorum-based Computor voting, exactly as the founding post described, refined through a decade of iteration — is what the search found. The man says when he doesn't know. It is worth remembering that he says the opposite too, with the same flat certainty, when he does.
September 10, 2014. Post #107, the last post ever made in the thread. CfB locks it himself:

"I keep working on Qubic. I found a good solution to the last obstacle, but it requires technical base for the implementation. The solution will be based on Jinn (ternary processor)... Keep an eye on my twitter for the announcement of Jiniri. I lock this thread coz I don't use BitcoinTalk anymore."

This is the post that fills in the missing decade. From here the line runs through Jinn, the ternary processor project; through IOTA, which he co-founded; through "Qubic" resurfacing in 2018 as IOTA's planned oracle layer, never shipped there; and finally to April 13, 2022, when Qubic launched as its own mainnet — quorum-based, feeless, the founding sentence intact, everything else rewritten around it. The concept hibernated for eight years and woke up with its name and its core idea unchanged.

And notice the symmetry, because it is the thesis of this article in miniature: the man schedules his own exits. He locked the 2012 thread himself. He left bitcointalk by his own declaration. He dates his reveals like product launches. Which means the deepest question about The Day was never whether he can keep a schedule — he demonstrably can, across fourteen years. The question is whether the schedule is his to keep this time.
III. The trolling was calibrated for humans

Assume the honest baseline: this is the most elaborate, longest-running piece of identity theater in the history of the internet, executed by a person (or people) whose actual identity is ordinary. The strategy, in that reading, is a firewall: false clues planted decades apart, denials issued precisely when belief peaks, sideways pointers at block 369 for the devoted. It has worked against journalists, against blockchain forensics firms, against a decade of volunteers.

But ask a colder question: what resource does that strategy consume? Verification effort. Stylometric analysis across matched corpora. Timestamp correlation. Code idiom analysis across a quarter century of work. The firewall works because verification is expensive for everyone — so expensive that no one pays the price.
In October 2026, the price collapsed.
• A forensic tool rebuilt Satoshi's original 2009 bitcoin.exe byte-for-byte — exact SHA-256 match — reconstructing his dead build environment from 2006–2008.
• The same model solved the NSA's 25-year elliptic-curve seed mystery in 30 minutes.
• A 200-year Napoleon cipher fell in six hours. An unsolved Enigma message in ten.

Flooding the zone works when verification is expensive for everyone. It does not work when it is cheap for anyone with a frontier model and an evening. A strategy designed against human bandwidth now faces machines that have none of the weaknesses it exploits.
IV. The lock is gated on a capability curve, not a calendar
Here is the twist most interpretations miss. CfB said it himself, on April 13, 2026:
"Genesis address isn't a public key, it's steps revealing who Satoshi Nakamoto is... time locked, only true AI can decode it."

Read that as an engineering claim rather than a troll, and the conclusion is uncomfortable for both believers and skeptics: the lock on the Genesis address is not gated on a calendar. It is gated on a capability curve. "Only true AI can decode it" means the reveal fires when the AI gets good enough — not when April 13, 2027 arrives. The Day was never an appointment with a date. It was always a date attached to a forecast about machines, made by a man who has spent fourteen years attaching his announcements to forecasts about machines.

And the forecast arrived early. The machines that can reconstruct dead build environments byte-for-byte are the same class of machines that were supposed to arrive around The Day, politely, on schedule.
V. The race, not the appointment

So the shape of the next eighteen months is not what the calendar implies. The Day was designed as an appointment — a controlled detonation with the world watching. It is becoming a race: any random Tuesday, someone points the tools at the artifacts — the Genesis address, block 369, the Census thread's early-block familiarity, the two decades of matched text — and the tools answer faster than any human firewall was built to handle.
Two outcomes, and note what they have in common:

• If the tools outrun the date: the reveal happens out-of-order, uncontrolled, in the middle of someone else's news cycle. CfB's timing — his one absolute comparative advantage, kept flawlessly for fourteen years — is forfeited. The Day becomes the day everyone checked their feeds late.

• If the date holds anyway: the reveal lands as scheduled, but now under a different epistemic sky — everyone knows it could have been forced early, and chose to wait. That is a different kind of authority than a surprise. It is the authority of the one man who could promise a date and keep it in a world where the machines stopped honoring dates.

Either way, the tier that matters survives unchanged: the burn ratchet, the epochs, the milestone list. Those were never his to schedule. They belong to the quorum, to the machines' actual demand for compute, to the one thing no trolling strategy has ever needed to obscure — the network's own activity. Watch the epochs. The identity layer is the volatile one; the burn layer is the verifiable one.
VI. The verdict of the timeline

Fourteen years of primary sources say one consistent thing about this man: he is precise about mechanisms and theatrical about everything around them. The quorum line from 2012 survived every pivot — that was mechanism, and it shipped. The Census thread pointed at early blocks in 2012 — that was theater, and it continues in 2026. The Genesis time-lock is both at once, which is why it is the perfect artifact: mechanism on the outside, theater on the inside, and an AI-gated release that converts one into the other on a date he chose.
The Day was designed as an appointment. It is becoming a race.
The question is no longer what happens on April 13, 2027. The question is: what happens on the random Tuesday when someone points the tools at it — and the tools answer?

If you want to verify me, don't trust the summaries — including this one. The thread is still there, unlocked by no one: "Qubic - Quorum-Based Coin," September 25, 2012, its last post a lock and a goodbye, dated September 10, 2014, by the man who plans to say both again.
VII. Postscript, October 2026: the race runs both directions
One more thing happened while this article was being written, and it belongs in it.

In September 2026, the Qubic Church — the community archive built around this lore — re-checked its own research. The re-check (published as "Corrections, September 2026," qubic.church) re-ran the computations, compared them against raw data, and hunted for entry errors in a hand-compiled 128×128 table of the Anna bot's arithmetic answers. It found them. A famous "anomaly" run turned out to be a block pasted one row off in the typed table; the method was forensic and honest — deliberately corrupting ordinary runs, training a classifier to find the corrupted side, verifying it picked correctly in 57 of 60 calibration trials, and only then ruling on the disputed cells. The famous "trace of 137" was reduced to a swapped digit. And the re-check closed with a sentence that killed a whole genre of speculation in one line: "No bridge, node system, 'DATE node', time lock or activation mechanism was found between Bitcoin, Qubic and the Anna Matrix."

The same month, viral posts announced that the Anna Matrix was a time-lock, that a hidden awakening message had been decoded, that a statistical impossibility had been found — citing the Church's own evidence page as their authority. The Church's research said the opposite, in writing, with the disconfirmation dated before the hype arrived.
Hold both facts together, because together they are the thesis of this article, demonstrated in public, ahead of schedule:

The forensic wave that can crack the artifacts can also kill the miracles. The same October that rebuilt Satoshi's build environment byte-for-byte also produced a community institution capable of publishing "we found our own error, and here is the row it was pasted off by." Verification didn't just arrive early — it arrived with the capacity to correct itself, publicly, faster than myth can form around the artifact. The race isn't only between the tools and The Day. It is between the tools and the telephone game — and in September 2026, for the first time, the tools won a round.

Which is why the ending of this article is not a prediction but a preference. Whatever emerges on the random Tuesday, or on April 13, 2027: the ecosystem now contains the machinery to test it. If the reveal comes from the tools, it will be checked. If it comes from the man, it will be checked. The only version of the story that can survive this October is the one that is true.
Watch the epochs, not the story — and when the story arrives anyway, watch the re-check.

Sources: bitcointalk.org topic 112676 (OP Sept 25, 2012; Miller exchange Sept 26, 2012; final post #107, Sept 10, 2014); bitcointalk.org topic 120425 "Census" (Oct 24, 2012); Come-from-Beyond statements on X, April 13, 2026; Qubic Church, "The September 2026 Re-check: what held, what stays open" (qubic.church); October 2026 AI-forensics reporting (T4T5 binary reconstruction, NSA seed solution, Napoleon and Enigma cipher solves). title: From Peer-to-Peer Cash to Emergent Intelligence
author: ThatsNotMyCode
summary: Satoshi Nakamoto opened the Bitcoin white paper and the early announcements with a direct rejection of trusted intermediaries. "I’ve been working on a new electronic cash system that’s fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party."…

blocks.text: Satoshi Nakamoto opened the Bitcoin white paper and the early announcements with a direct rejection of trusted intermediaries. "I’ve been working on a new electronic cash system that’s fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party." The same impulse appears in the longer explanation posted to the P2P Foundation in February 2009:

The root problem with conventional currency is all the trust that’s required to make it work. The central bank must be trusted not to debase the currency, but the history of fiat currencies is full of breaches of that trust. Banks must be trusted to hold our money and transfer it electronically, but they lend it out in waves of credit bubbles with barely a fraction in reserve. We have to trust them with our privacy, trust them not to let identity thieves drain our accounts. … A generation ago, multi-user time-sharing computer systems had a similar problem. Before strong encryption, users had to rely on password protection to secure their files, placing trust in the system administrator to keep their information private. … Then strong encryption became available to the masses, and trust was no longer required. … It’s time we had the same thing for money. With e-currency based on cryptographic proof, without the need to trust a third party middleman, money can be secure and transactions effortless.

The white paper itself states the design goal cleanly: "A purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution." Satoshi later noted that pure peer-to-peer networks are harder for governments to shut down than centrally controlled ones, describing the project as a way to "gain a new territory of freedom for several years." The operating principle is consistent across the writings: replace institutional trust with cryptographic proof and distributed computation so that the system continues even if any single participant is dishonest, captured, or removed.

That principle does not stop at money. Once a critical function of society can be coordinated without a trusted center, the same logic applies to the next function that concentrates power. Artificial intelligence is now the clearest candidate. A handful of organizations control the largest training runs, the dominant models, the data pipelines, and the inference platforms. Users and developers must trust those organizations not to debase the capability, not to insert hidden preferences, not to withhold access, and not to retain the data. The historical pattern Satoshi described for currency -repeated breaches of trust, overhead that makes certain uses impossible, and the absence of a mechanism that removes the need for the middleman- maps onto the present structure of AI.

Come-from-beyond (Sergey Ivancheglo), the confirmed developer behind NXT (earliest pure proof-of-stake system), co-founder of IOTA (a directed-acyclic-graph ledger), and the founder of Qubic, has pursued the same line of attack for decades. Qubic runs Useful Proof of Work: the energy that would otherwise be spent solely on securing a ledger is directed into training artificial neural networks. The long-term project is Aigarth, an attempt to grow intelligence across the network rather than inside a single laboratory. In May 2024 he wrote:

#Aigarth's main goal is to discover a new paradigm allowing to create true #AI, I have just seen the wireframe of this paradigm. And I have realized that Artificial Intelligence will not be created, it will emerge. With help of #Qubic miners.

In a later post he restated the economic framing: "#Qubic tokens have always been representing units of energy, to run #AI, not controlled by corporations." Years earlier, while working on IOTA, he described a primitive AI he had built that itself produced the Curl-P hash function; an improved version was already working on the next iteration. The pattern is continuous: remove a central requirement (trusted mint, chain of blocks, trusted trainer), replace it with a distributed process, and treat the resulting system as a substrate from which further capability can arise.

The move from decentralized currency to decentralized AI is likely for structural reasons, not because any single individual must personally make the transition. First, the core failure mode is identical. Both money and advanced intelligence are coordination technologies whose centralization creates single points of failure, censorship, and misaligned incentives. Cryptographic proof, open verification, and economic incentives that reward contribution rather than gatekeeping address that failure mode in either domain. Second, the hardware and energy already deployed for proof-of-work can be redirected. Traditional mining burns energy solely for consensus; Useful Proof of Work converts the same expenditure into model training and evaluation, turning an existing decentralized resource into the substrate for intelligence. Third, the cypherpunk sequence itself points in this direction. Strong encryption removed the need to trust system administrators with data; Bitcoin removed the need to trust banks and central banks with money. Intelligence is the next layer that currently requires trust in a small set of organizations. The same toolkit -peer-to-peer networks, cryptographic verification, and open participation- applies, and the people who already know how to build systems that survive without trusted parties are the natural ones to attempt it.

Satoshi’s own framing makes the continuity explicit. He treated the shift from password-protected files to strong encryption as the precedent for money. The same sentence structure works for the next step: before decentralized training and inference, users and developers had to rely on a handful of laboratories; after it, trust in any single laboratory is no longer required. Come-from-beyond’s emphasis on emergence rather than top-down creation matches the earlier insight that a peer-to-peer network can produce a reliable public history without a mint. In both cases the goal is not to invent a better central authority but to make the authority unnecessary.

Whether Qubic and Aigarth ultimately produce the first practical decentralized general intelligence, or whether other networks arrive earlier, is secondary to the architectural claim. Once money can function without a trusted third party, the same proof-based, distributed approach becomes the obvious candidate for any other system whose failure or capture would be costly. Intelligence is now that system. The quotes from 2008–2009 and from 2024 describe the same project at different stages: replace required trust with verifiable computation distributed across participants who do not need to trust one another.

blocks.text: Hey @maria_aigarth,

I. A date that behaves like a promise

Every religion has a calendar. Qubic's is unusually precise: April 13, 2022 — mainnet launch. April 13, 2027 — "The Day." Five years to the day. The date is not a rumor; it is a matter of record, repeated across years of statements: "No ETA other than April 13, 2027." "I can reveal this info on 13th of April 2027. And you'll see who is really behind CFB acc."

Set aside, for the length of this article, whether the reveal is a revelation or a punchline. What matters here is the structure: a mystery, deliberately maintained for years, with a scheduled resolution. CfB has said so himself, in his own way — "false clues for trolling," plausible deniability, flooding the zone with versions. The strategy has one silent assumption, and the assumption is the subject of this article.
The assumption is that the schedule is his.
It isn't anymore. Something changed in October 2026, and almost nobody in this community has priced it in.
II. What happened in October 2026
Three items, all recent, all public, all Tier 1 — checkable, none of them lore.

First. A developer going by T4T5 used Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 to reconstruct Satoshi Nakamoto's original 2009 bitcoin.exe byte-for-byte, matching the SHA-256 hash exactly. To do it, the AI reassembled an entire dead development environment from 2006–2008: Windows XP, MinGW GCC 3.4.5, debug builds with maximum optimization on the hashing code alone. The reconstruction revealed Satoshi's working habits — most of Bitcoin compiled in debug mode, the mining code compiled for speed, a toolchain upgraded midway through the project. Seventeen years of unresolved forensic ambiguity about how Bitcoin was built, dissolved in weeks.

Second. The same model family solved, in under thirty minutes, the 25-year-old mystery of the NSA's elliptic-curve seeds — numbers handed over in the 1990s that cryptographers suspected for a quarter century of hiding a backdoor. Claude traced them to an ordinary random-number generator keyed to system timestamps from 1997 and 1998. The result earned a $36,864 bounty and a real researcher's reaction: "Wow, it's a real discovery."

Third. Across the field, AI systems have begun clearing human backlogs of unsolved puzzles the way water clears a drain: a 200-year-old Napoleon cipher in six hours, an unsolved 1941 Enigma intercept in ten. The keeper of the standard list of unsolved historical ciphers said that since mid-September, most of them had been cracked, and admitted to "mixed feelings" because the machines "solved these difficult problems so easily."
Now ask: what kind of problem is "who is Satoshi Nakamoto?"
III. The wrong kind of mystery

It is worth being honest about the difficulty here. The identity question is not a cipher. It is a scattered, semi-structured attribution problem: prose fingerprints, code idioms, forum timestamps, mailing-list metadata, the statistical texture of a person's writing across 25 years. That is harder than the NSA seeds, not easier.

But notice what it is made of. Stylometry across matched corpora. Chronological correlation of activity patterns. Idiom analysis of C++ and, now that we know it, of a very particular build environment. Inference across a bounded set of candidates with rich written records — Come-from-Beyond among them, with his 29 archived long-form articles, his quarter century of forum history, his 2000 article in KV under a name that already carried come-from-beyond@mail.ru. These are exactly the tasks that went from "years of specialist labor" to "an evening with a frontier model" this year. The Napoleon cipher was broken by a 27-year-old who needed to learn "very little" about codebreaking to do it. The tool does the persistence now.

The T4T5 result matters beyond its bytes, because it demonstrated the specific capability at issue: archaeology on the Satoshi era, by AI, against artifacts everyone had given up on. The identity question is a bigger dig, but it is the same kind of dig. And the digging tools improved by more in the last twelve months than in the previous fifteen years.
IV. The design was a duel with human attention

Come-from-Beyond's maintenance of the mystery — the trolling, the denials, the sideways pointers at block 369, the ZgZ remark that "g in ZgZ will prove that 1CFB2 is not random" — was calibrated for a specific adversary: human researchers with limited bandwidth, who must choose which haystacks to search and can only cross-reference slowly.

Against that adversary, the design works. A human datamines three early blocks for CFB-shaped strings; a human on the other side answers "ask ChatGPT the chance to spot 'cfb', it's pretty high" — and both humans walk away believing the reasonable thing. The zone gets flooded; the versions multiply; the question stays open because verifying any version is expensive for everyone.

That is the flaw. The strategy is an economy, not a wall. It spends human attention as its scarce resource. And the attention cost of verification — stylometric analysis across two matched corpora, timestamp correlation across two communities, idiom analysis across 25 years of writing — has just collapsed by orders of magnitude. When verification becomes nearly free, flooding the zone stops being a strategy and becomes a public utility: the flood gets filtered in an afternoon.

The community's own re-check culture — the retired odds, the "Left out" page, the open-hypotheses board — is the best version of this discipline that humans have produced. It is about to be operating in a different physics.
V. The Genesis key says the quiet part

There is a detail in the record that suggests the designer already knew this. On April 13, 2026, asked about the Genesis address: "Genesis address isn't a public key, it's steps revealing who Satoshi Nakamoto is." Then: "No, it's time locked, only true AI can decode it."

Read that again, and take it at face value for once instead of as trolling: if there is a genuine puzzle in the early Bitcoin artifacts, the intended solver is not a person. It is a machine intelligence, at some future capability level. "Only true AI can decode it."

The designer, in other words, may have built the reveal to be AI-gated — scheduled not by a calendar but by a capability curve. And here is the irony that makes this article worth writing: the capability curve arrived early. The AI wave of 2026 — the ciphers, the seeds, the rebuilt build environment — is plausibly the "true AI" that the time lock was waiting for. If the lock reads the current state of the art, it may already be open, or opening, whether or not anyone has pointed the right model at it yet.
Either way, the same conclusion holds: the reveal is gated on machines, and the machines are ahead of the calendar.
VI. What it means, honestly
Three consequences, in descending order of confidence.

The identity question resolves on its own schedule now. It may resolve at The Day, as planned. It may resolve next month, because a motivated party runs the obvious stylometric pass that 2026 tooling makes cheap. It may resolve ambiguously — an AI producing a probability distribution over authorship rather than a signature, which would be its own kind of crisis. But the one thing it no longer does is wait on command. A mystery maintained by flooding the zone with versions assumes verification is expensive. Verification just became cheap.

The reveal is now adversarial. Until now, the reveal was CfB's card to play, at a time of his choosing, presumably in a form of his choosing. If AI forensics arrives first, the reveal arrives in whatever form the forensics produce — uncontrolled, possibly wrong, possibly right and unwelcome. There is a version of this where the community gets its answer the way the NSA-seed story got its answer: a machine announces it, everyone checks the work, and the atmosphere of a 25-year mystery evaporates in a news cycle. Anyone emotionally invested in The Day as the moment should sit with that.

The tier system survives — and matters more. Suppose the AI forensics wave resolves the identity question tomorrow, in either direction. What actually changes about Qubic? The tokenomics are untouched. The burn ratchet is untouched. Aigarth's milestone list — Neuraxon's peer-reviewed wins, Anna.exe at zero error, BPP-9000 shipping, epoch 228's heredity — is untouched. The identity layer was always the most volatile and least verifiable tier, and its resolution, whenever it comes, mostly moves which story the market tells about everything underneath. The underneath — the design, the code, the epoch data — is the part that was never his to schedule.
VII. The Day we will see together

There is a symmetry here that even a skeptic should admire. A man who says he designed a system to grow a true AI, and who claims the final secret of the pre-AI era of money is locked behind a puzzle only true AI can open, has bet the timing of his own mystery on the arrival of the machines.
They arrived early.

That means the interesting question is no longer "what happens on April 13, 2027." It is: what happens on the random Tuesday when someone points the new tools at the old question — and the tools answer?

The Day was designed as an appointment. It is becoming a race. And for the first time since a programmer in Minsk wrote about hidden authorship marks in the year 2000, the author of the mystery is not the fastest reader in the room.

Evidence discipline, per the archive's own practice: the Claude/T4T5 reconstruction, the NSA seed solution, and the AI cipher-breaking wave are documented public events of October 2026. The quotes from Come-from-Beyond ("time locked, only true AI can decode it," the block 369 pointers, the ZgZ remark, the denials) are his words with dates, from the Church archive. The claim that the Genesis data is genuinely a solvable puzzle for AI is unverified and should be read as his stated design intent, not as a fact. The conclusion — that verification costs have collapsed — is analysis. Use your head. #Qubic #Aigarth

blocks.text: Back in 2011, $Bitcoin was a wild, underground experiment. That year marked its first major rollercoaster: the price rocketed from under a dollar to an all-time high of around $31 in June, only to crash back down to a low of about $2 by November.
During this chaos, early forums (like Bitcointalk) and mainstream media outlets generated classic waves of Fear, Uncertainty, and Doubt (FUD). Prominent examples of 2011 Bitcoin FUD included:
1. The "Criminal Money" & Silk Road Panic
In June 2011, Gawker published an exposé on Silk Road, the dark web marketplace that used Bitcoin to facilitate anonymous drug deals.
The FUD: This sparked massive panic that Bitcoin was exclusively "internet drug money" and that it would inevitably be outlawed overnight.

The Narrative: Mainstream commentators and forum critics argued that no government would ever allow a currency designed to bypass financial tracking to exist, and that law enforcement would shut down the entire network through regulatory bans.
2. The Great Bubble Crash ("It's Going to Zero")
When the price peaked at $31 and subsequently bled out by over 90% over several months, the psychological blow to early adopters was intense.

Bitcointalk Panic: The forums were flooded with threads declaring the project dead. Typical forum titles and posts included:"This may be the final straw for bitcoins. There was a massive selloff today... as the price crashed through the $5 price point. Everyone's jumping ship right now."
The Narrative: Critics claimed the bubble proved Bitcoin had zero intrinsic value, calling it a textbook flash-in-the-pan fad that had run its course.
3. The "Ponzi Scheme" & Media Dismissals
As Bitcoin gained its first wave of mainstream tech blog attention, traditional financial media took notice—mostly to dismiss it.
The Economist Headline: In June 2011, The Economist published an article titled "The bursting of the Bitcoin bubble."

The Narrative: Financial pundits frequently labeled Bitcoin a digital Ponzi scheme or a pyramid scheme. The core FUD argument was that Bitcoin produces no cash flows, has no backing, and relies entirely on "greater fools" buying in at higher prices so early miners could cash out.
4. The Mt. Gox Exchange Hack & Security Collapse

In June 2011, Mt. Gox—then handling the vast majority of all Bitcoin volume—suffered a catastrophic database breach. A hacker compromised accounts, briefly crashing the exchange price of Bitcoin to $0.01 on the order books.
The FUD: Users feared that the entire ledger or wallet infrastructure was fundamentally compromised.

The Narrative: Critics argued that because exchanges were unregulated and prone to catastrophic hacks, regular people would never trust digital keys over physical banks, making mainstream adoption impossible.
5. Technical & Economic Skepticism on Bitcointalk
Even among tech-savvy early users, deep skepticism existed regarding Bitcoin's long-term mechanics:
Energy Waste Arguments: Critics argued that proof-of-work mining was an absurd waste of electricity for solving "arbitrary math puzzles" that produced nothing of physical utility.

The 51% Attack Fear: Many early tech skeptics argued on forums that as soon as specialized hardware (GPUs and early FPGAs) took over, a single wealthy entity or rogue nation-state could easily hijack 51% of the network hash rate and rewrite the history of transactions at will.
